'''Sir Arnold Whittaker Wolfendale'''<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1977%2F39%27) |title=Library and Archive Catalogue Wolfendale |publisher=[[The Royal Society]] |archive-date=19 December 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20131219104739/http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo=='EC/1977/39') |location=London }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ellis|first1=Richard S.|last2=Watson|first2=Alan A.|title=Sir Arnold Whittaker Wolfendale. 25 June 1927—21 December 2020|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|year=2022|volume=72|pages=407–430|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2021.0028|s2cid=245355111|doi-access=free}}</ref> (25 June 1927 – 21 December 2020) was a British astronomer who served as the fourteenth [[Astronomer Royal]] from 1991<ref>''The London Gazette'', 8 February 1991, Issue 52444 Page [https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/52444/page/2061 2061]</ref> to 1995. He was Professor of Physics at [[Durham University]] from 1965 until 1992<ref name="durhamuni">{{cite web |url=https://www.dur.ac.uk/physics/staff/profiles/?id=1822 |title=Prof Sir AW Wolfendale - Durham University |publisher=[[Durham University]] |archive-date=20 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131220040811/https://www.dur.ac.uk/physics/staff/profiles/?id=1822 |access-date=19 December 2013 }}</ref> and served as president of the [[European Physical Society]] (1999–2001).<ref name="debretts">[http://www.debretts.com/people/biographies/browse/w/4565/Arnold+Whittaker.aspx Prof Sir Arnold Wolfendale, Debretts Biography]  {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131102163902/http://www.debretts.com/people/biographies/browse/w/4565/Arnold%2BWhittaker.aspx |date=2 November 2013 }}</ref> He was president of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] from 1981 to 1983.<ref>Royal Astronomical Society: [https://ras.ac.uk/about-the-ras/79-general/766-past-ras-presidents Past RAS Presidents]</ref>

==Education and background==
Wolfendale was born in [[Rugby, Warwickshire]] on 25 June 1927.<ref name="whoswho">{{cite web |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U40459/ |title=WOLFENDALE, Sir Arnold (Whittaker) |work=Who's Who 2013, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2013; online edn, Oxford University Press }}{{subscription required}}</ref><ref name="gro">GRO Register of Births: SEP 1927 6d 1198a RUGBY – Arnold W. Wolfendale, mmn = Hoyle</ref> His family moved to [[Flixton, Greater Manchester|Flixton]], [[Lancashire]] when he was 18 months. He attended [[Stretford Grammar School]] near Manchester. Wolfendale graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in physics from the [[University of Manchester]] in 1948, followed by a [[PhD]] in 1953<ref name="wolfendalephd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Arnold|last=Wolfendale |title=The nuclear interactions of mu-mesons |publisher=University of Manchester |date=1953 |url=http://www.theses.com|author-link=Arnold Wolfendale}}{{subscription required}}</ref> and a [[Doctor of Science]] in 1970.

==Career==
During his career he held academic posts at the universities of [[University of Manchester]] (1951–6), [[Durham University]] (1956–92), the [[University of Ceylon]] and the [[University of Hong Kong]].  He was Professor of Physics at Durham 1965–92, including a period as head of department, and remained an [[emeritus]] professor until his death.

In 1965, he was part of the team that first detected [[neutrino]]s at the [[Kolar Gold Fields]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ellis|first1=Richard S.|last2=Watson|first2=Alan A.|title=Sir Arnold Whittaker Wolfendale. 25 June 1927—21 December 2020|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|year=2022|volume=72|pages=407–430|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2021.0028|s2cid=245355111|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Wolfendale was elected a fellow of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] in 1973, and a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1977.<ref name="royal"/> He served as Astronomer Royal from 1991 to 1995. In 1992, Wolfendale retired from teaching, and he was knighted in 1995. In 1996 he became professor of experimental physics with the [[Royal Institution of Great Britain]]. A lecture theatre in Durham University's new Calman Learning Centre has been named in his honour. He was an honorary DSc of Bucharest University and foreign member of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. His nomination for the Royal Society reads{{centered pull quote|Distinguished for his many contributions to the study of the cosmic radiation through a wide-ranging series of experimental investigations and critical analyses of cosmic ray data. Well known for his development of two novel techniques: the neon flash tube, a visual detector of great stability used widely in spectrographs and cosmic ray neutrino and quark studies, and the 'solid iron' spectrograph. Internationally recognised as the leading authority on muon spectra and charge ratios at ground level and at various depths underground in the energy range 5 x 10 [to the power of] 8-10 [to the power of 13] eV, measurements which are among the most basic data of cosmic rays. Measured the spectra of cosmic ray protons, neutrons and pions and from these data and the muon spectrum determined the primary spectrum and K/pi ratio. Results on the interactions of muons were of importance in a number of other investigations, e.g. in the Davis experiment on solar neutrinos. Introduction of the neon flash tube technique to the Indian and South African experiments on cosmic ray neutrinos was decisive and led to the clear identification of neutrino interactions and the determination of the cross section as a function of energy. Has established recently fine astrophysical groups in Durham which have already made useful contributions to the theory of the propagation of cosmic rays in the galaxy, to the explanation of the ultra-high energy end of the primary spectrum and to the origin of the gamma-ray background radiation. His optical group under Scarrott has recently obtained a beautiful map of the galaxy M82 in Rayleigh scattered light, and from it an accurate position for the luminous nucleus.<ref name="royal"/>}}

== Other activities ==

In 1992 Wolfendale became patron of the [[Society for Popular Astronomy]] and was a keen supporter of its activities. He opened [[Kielder Observatory]], Northumberland in 2008,<ref>Kielder Observatory: [https://kielderobservatory.org/our-observatory Our Observatory]</ref> and was its Patron.<ref>[https://kielderobservatory.org/page/3/ Kielder Observatory: Astrophotography Competition]</ref> In 2009 he was the 156th president of the [[Birmingham and Midland Institute]].<ref name="bmi">{{Citation |title=The BMI President |url=https://bmi.org.uk/the-bmi-president/ |access-date=2021-02-08}}</ref> From April 2013, he was one of the two honorary vice presidents of the [[Society for the History of Astronomy]].<ref>[https://societyforthehistoryofastronomy.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/shabulletin24.pdf Society for the History of Astronomy Newsletter [Bulletin<nowiki>]</nowiki>, Issue 24, Spring 2015], p50 [pdf]</ref>

== Personal life ==
He married Audrey Darby in 1951. They had twin sons. His wife Audrey died in 2007. He married anthropologist Dorothy Middleton, at Durham Cathedral, on 5 September 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/13709379.Renowned_academics_tie_knot_at_cathedral_wedding/|title=Renowned academics tie knot at cathedral wedding|last=Unwin|first=Bruce|date=9 September 2015|website=The Northern Echo|access-date= 11 July 2017}}</ref> Wolfendale died in December 2020 at the age of 93.<ref>[https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2021/01/03/professor-sir-arnold-wolfendale-former-astronomer-royal-probed/ Professor Sir Arnold Wolfendale, former Astronomer Royal who probed the source of cosmic rays – obituary]</ref><ref name="Times_30_Dec_2020">''The Times'', 30 December 2020, p49 (Subscription required)</ref>
